Contrast tests neural responses to receiving romantic interest (yes) vs rejection (no) in a speed-dating task — a clear social processing effect at the contrast level.

The contrast indexes social reward/affiliation, not communicative signal exchange; it does not isolate communication variables.
Contrast does not explicitly isolate self-referential processing (self vs other or self-evaluation); it primarily indexes partner decision effects rather than self-specific processes.

Unsigned prediction errors from an RL model of partner decisions index surprise about social feedback and learning — a social processing effect.
The unsigned prediction-error regressor indexes surprise/learning about partner choices rather than directly isolating attachment/bonding measures.
This analysis models learning/prediction-error signals about partner decisions, not communicative signal exchange.

Unsigned prediction errors reflect learning about the participant's own desirability and personal social-image; the authors interpret RMPFC activity as social prediction errors tied to the personal self—this isolates self-relevant learning.

Contrast compares partner faces given 'yes' vs 'no' (anticipation of partner decision) — clearly a social task-evoked contrast.
